description: A financial institution that provides banking services (nostro/vostro accounts, wire transfers, trade finance, FX) to another financial institution (the respondent). Correspondents are essential for international payments. Subject to enhanced due diligence under AMLR Art. 38.

The financial institution receiving correspondent banking services from a correspondent bank. The correspondent extends credit and payment services to the respondent. AML risk: correspondent cannot monitor end-customers of respondent bank.

Nostro account: 'our account held by you' — account maintained by a correspondent at another bank. Vostro account: 'your account held by us' — the same account from the other bank's perspective. Core infrastructure of correspondent banking.

A correspondent account through which the respondent bank's customers can conduct transactions directly, as if they have an account at the correspondent bank. Higher AML risk than standard correspondent accounts — end customers are essentially invisible to the correspondent.

Where a respondent bank provides correspondent services to sub-respondent banks through its own correspondent accounts. Creates multi-layer opacity: the top-level correspondent has no visibility of sub-respondents or their customers. High-risk structure.

Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. Provides secure messaging for financial transactions between banks globally. SWIFT exclusion (Russia 2022) is a major sanctions enforcement tool. SWIFT messages carry originator/beneficiary information under TFR.

Unique identifier for banks in SWIFT messages. 8-11 character alphanumeric code identifying institution, country, location, and branch. Used in correspondent banking to identify parties. Required in TFR Travel Rule data.

Practice by which financial institutions exit or restrict business relationships with entire categories of customers, countries, or business types to avoid perceived AML/sanctions risk, rather than managing that risk proportionately. Concern of FATF, BIS, FSB, and IMF.

De-risking reduces access to financial services in developing countries and for money services businesses, remittance providers, and NGOs. FATF and World Bank data show significant withdrawal of CBR relationships in Africa, Pacific, Caribbean. Creates unbanked populations.

EDD process required under AMLR Art. 38 for correspondent relationships: (1) Gather information on respondent's business, reputation, supervisory framework; (2) Assess adequacy of AML/CFT controls; (3) Obtain senior management approval; (4) Document respective responsibilities; (5) Annual review; (6) Prohibit shell bank relationships.

Process of assigning risk scores to correspondent banking relationships considering: country risk, regulatory quality of respondent jurisdiction, respondent ownership structure, product/service complexity, volume and nature of transactions, AML/CFT framework of respondent.

Periodic review of correspondent banking relationships required under AMLR. Must include updated due diligence on the respondent, review of documented responsibilities, assessment of any adverse findings or regulatory actions against the respondent.

Decision process for terminating a correspondent banking relationship: escalation to senior management, documentation of reasons, regulatory notification requirements, orderly wind-down period, consideration of financial inclusion impact. Must not create 'de-risking' without proportionate risk assessment.

Industry principles for correspondent banking from the Wolfsberg Group (13 major international banks). Cover: respondent due diligence, CBDDQ questionnaire, documentation, ongoing monitoring, and exit. Widely adopted as industry standard.

Standardised questionnaire developed by Wolfsberg Group for gathering AML/CFT information from respondent banks. Covers: legal and regulatory basis, ownership, governance, AML programme, high-risk products, customer types, and correspondent banking exposure. Industry standard tool.

AMLR Art. 38 requires credit institutions to apply EDD for correspondent relationships with third-country respondents: gather information on the respondent's AML/CFT controls, document each party's AML responsibilities, senior management approval, prohibit shell bank relationships, and prohibit payable-through accounts with shell banks.

FATF Recommendation 13 requires countries to ensure financial institutions apply special measures to cross-border correspondent banking: customer due diligence on respondent institution, assessment of AML controls, prohibition of shell bank relationships, and documentation of responsibilities.

Correspondent banking EDD obligations sit in AMLR Art. 38 (formerly AMLD4 Art. 19). Article requires specific EDD elements beyond standard CDD. Shell bank prohibition is absolute — not risk-based. Documentation of AML responsibilities between correspondent and respondent is mandatory.

Correspondent banks process wire transfers subject to TFR Travel Rule. Correspondent banks must check that originator/beneficiary information accompanies transfers and take appropriate action (including SAR) if information is missing.

Sanctions enforcement heavily relies on correspondent banking. Russia's SWIFT disconnection (2022) is the most significant use of correspondent banking as a sanctions enforcement tool. Iran has been excluded from SWIFT since 2012 (with brief suspension 2016-2019). Respondent sanctions screening is a CBR EDD requirement.

Basel Committee on Banking Supervision paper 264 (2016) on sound management of risks related to money laundering and financing of terrorism for correspondent banking. Establishes sound practices for CDD on respondents.

MSBs (money transfer operators, currency exchangers, crypto exchanges) face difficulty accessing banking services due to de-risking. FATF guidance emphasises that MSBs should be able to access banking services through proportionate risk management, not blanket exclusions.

FSB, IMF, World Bank, and FATF established a joint group to monitor and address decline in CBRs. Publishes annual data on CBR trends. Finds continued decline, particularly for small island developing states, Pacific, and Caribbean.
